94.title: The Melchizedek Teachings in the Orient
94.b0.ask: “How was the Salem gospel — that God’s favor is received by faith — taken up in India, China, and East Asia, and how was it clouded over?”
94.b2.p: In Paper 93 we saw how Machiventa Melchizedek left the covenant of faith at Salem and trained his missionaries. Paper 94 now follows those missionaries eastward, to India, China, Japan, and Tibet.
94.b3.p: The teachers of Salem went out to the most remote tribes of Africa and Eurasia, preaching Machiventa’s gospel: that belief and trust in one universal God is the only price of obtaining divine favor. They set up training centers everywhere and made local converts into teachers of their own peoples.
94.b4.p: What did this simple gospel leave behind when it met the ancient religions and philosophies of the East? And what blocked its way and led it astray?
94.b5.q: ⟦Q 94:12.7⟧The hour is striking for presenting to Buddhism, to Christianity, to Hinduism, even to the peoples of all faiths, not the gospel about Jesus, but the living, spiritual reality of the gospel of Jesus.⟦/Q⟧
94.b7.h: 1. The Salem Teachings in Vedic India
94.b8.p: In Melchizedek’s day, India had just come under the rule of the Aryan-Andites who had entered from the northwest. The Vedic gods were what remained of an original belief in one God that had broken apart, tribe by tribe, into many; at this time they were being gathered again into a single pantheon. Ideas of a Father-God, such as Prajapati or Brahma, were also arising.
94.b9.p: The one God preached by the Salem missionaries did not differ too much from this concept, but the Salem doctrine, which had no rituals, clashed head-on with the teachings of the Brahman priests. The Brahmans would never accept the teaching that favor is received by faith, apart from sacrifices, and this rejection was a great turning point for India. To oppose the Salem teachers they gathered their sacred records and compiled the Rig-Veda. The Vedas contain both the loftiest and the most debased concepts of Deity.
94.b11.p: The book explains that the caste system was created to preserve Aryan identity; it failed to save the race, but it did keep the Brahman class alive. Under threat, the Brahmans exalted themselves to a place alongside the gods as a fundamental principle of the universe — something, the book says, that the priests of no other people ever went so far as to do.
94.b12.p: Added to this was the doctrine of endless reincarnation, the transmigration of souls, and people lost the hope of release and spiritual progress after death. The only way out became escape from self forever, by union with Brahman, and desire and ambition were denied. In trying to remove human elements from their idea of God, the Brahmans fell into the error of depersonalizing him, arriving not at the Paradise Father but at a distant and impersonal Absolute.
94.b13.q: ⟦Q 94:2.4⟧Of all civilizations, the Vedic-Aryan paid the most terrible price for its rejection of the Salem gospel.⟦/Q⟧
94.b15.p: The book regards Brahmanism at its height as one of the noblest achievements of the human mind in philosophy and metaphysics. Yet two essentials of religion were missing: the existence of the Universal Father, and the cosmic ascent to him. Brahman could be known only by denying every finite quality, so no believer could ever experience him personally.
94.b16.t: How it came close to truth, and what it missed
Close to the Supreme Being, but with no personal approach
Close to the summing up of deeds in the Supreme, but personality is swallowed up
Close to the indwelling Adjuster, but it denies human individuality
Like the Adjuster’s return, but there is no surviving morontia soul
It failed to distinguish the absolute, transcendental, and finite levels
94.b17.p: Its most fatal flaw was that it had no idea of the survival of something new and unique born of the union of the human will and God’s — the morontia counterpart of mortal personality. Nor did it recognize the personality of the Universal Father, who can be met personally on every level.
94.b19.p: As time passed, the masses of India returned to the old Vedic rituals, influenced by Melchizedek and fixed in form by the Brahmans. This oldest and most cosmopolitan of the world’s religions kept changing under the influence of Buddhism, Jainism, Islam, and Christianity. But the teachings of Jesus arrived so Occidentalized that they seemed strange, like a white man’s religion. Hindu theology pictures Deity on four levels.
94.b20.t: The Absolute, the Infinite One, the IT IS
The supreme trinity of Brahma, Siva, and Vishnu
Secondary gods such as Agni, Indra, and Soma
Supermen, heroes, demons, ghosts, fairies, and saints
94.b21.p: The strength of Hinduism is that it is the most adaptable and tolerant of religions. Woven into the daily life of the people without any great institution, it has survived. The book says that what India needs most today is the gospel of Jesus stripped of Western dogma: the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, lived out in loving service.
94.b22.h: 5. The Struggle for Truth in China
94.b23.p: The Salem missionaries reached China in the middle of the second millennium before Christ, and for over a hundred years they trained teachers at their headquarters at Si Fuch. The result was an early Taoism very different from the Taoism of today.
94.b24.t: Survived as the concept of Shang-ti, the God of heaven
The Most High Creator, who bestows favor in response to faith
The concept of the Absolute and the longing to escape from evil
94.b25.p: This blended faith became Shinto in Japan, and there too people came to know of Melchizedek’s coming in the flesh. The Chinese were the first people to free themselves from bondage to priests and from the fear of ghosts, but they went no further and fell into the error of ancestor worship. Still, the labors of Salem were not in vain; they became the moral and spiritual roots of Lao-tse and Confucius.
94.b27.p: About six hundred years before Michael’s coming, the teachings of Melchizedek were in danger of being buried beneath older beliefs and lost. Then, in the sixth century before Christ, the Salem gospel was revived as never before, through a number of human teachers.
94.b28.t: Tao is the One First Cause of all creation; man’s destiny is everlasting union with Tao
Returning good for evil, the faith of a little child, acting without coercing
Morality in place of magic; order on earth reflects the order of heaven
Brotherhood founded not on duty but on the love of God
94.b29.q: ⟦Q 94:6.6⟧The Absolute Deity does not strive but is always victorious; he does not coerce mankind but always stands ready to respond to their true desires⟦/Q⟧
94.b30.p: Lao-tse’s teachings have been almost forgotten in the East, and they bear little likeness to popular Taoism today. The writings of Confucius became the moral foundation for a third of mankind, but they also made order itself into a new fetish that held back the spirit of inquiry. In the end both men were exalted as gods, and China slipped back for a time into a theology swarming with demons and dragons.
94.b32.p: In the same age, Gautama Siddhartha appeared in India. He was heir to the chief of a small mountain valley, and after six fruitless years of yoga practice he laid the foundations of his own thinking. He stood against caste, asceticism, and reincarnation and sought to free people from fear, but he did not know the personality of the one universal Being.
94.b33.p: At Benares his disciple Bautan passed on to him the tradition of Melchizedek’s covenant with Abraham, and Gautama took an advanced position on salvation through faith. He sent out his disciples by sixties to proclaim the good news of a salvation freely given. But in his old age he wavered and told them to work out their own salvation. The book says that just as modern Christianity is not the original teaching of Jesus, modern Buddhism is not the true teaching of Gautama.
94.b35.p: To become a Buddhist one had only to profess faith in the Buddha, the Doctrine, and the Brotherhood. Gautama never made superhuman claims for himself, but his followers called him the enlightened one, the Buddha.
94.b36.t: Suffering, its origin, its ending, and the way to its ending
Right views, aspirations, speech, conduct, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, and contemplation
Against killing, stealing, unchastity, lying, and intoxicating drink
94.b37.p: Gautama did not ask men to destroy all desire; he wanted them to see how vain it is to place their hopes only on temporal goals. But his original teaching had neither divine help nor saving faith; it held that salvation is won by human effort alone. The book judges that his great truth was his proclamation of a universe of absolute justice, and that his greatest weakness was the failure to build a religion of unselfish social service.
94.b39.p: Buddhism represented the truths of Melchizedek better than any other religion of East Asia. Over twenty-five years King Asoka trained and sent out more than seventeen thousand missionaries, and within a single generation Buddhism became the leading religion of half the world. But the Buddhism that spread was no longer Gautama’s simple doctrine; it was a gospel of miracles that made him a god.
94.b40.t: After a thousand years it was absorbed by Brahmanism and disappeared
The Hinayana, the lesser way, which kept the early doctrines
The Mahayana, the greater way, freed from social limitations
Influenced by Taoism, Shinto, and Christianity
94.b41.p: Even so, Buddhism has kept high moral values and is still a living, growing religion, and those who believe this philosophy live better lives than many who do not.
94.b43.p: In Tibet the teachings of Melchizedek became mixed in the strangest way with Buddhism, Hinduism, Taoism, and Christianity. Bells and incense and rosaries, holy water and vestments, monks and a hierarchy under the grand lama, confession and purgatory, even prayer wheels — elements of every religion gathered into a ritual almost too heavy to bear. The book says the Tibetans have elements of every major religion except the simple gospel of Jesus: sonship with God and the brotherhood of man.
94.b45.p: When Buddhism entered China it mixed with ancestor worship and Taoist rituals, and the legends of miracles that made Gautama a god held great appeal for the Mahayana audience. But the teaching of the living Buddha bound Buddhism once more to the very rituals and incantations Gautama had fought against.
94.b46.p: The great advance of Buddhist philosophy was its understanding of the relativity of all truth: the small truth was for little minds, the large truth for great minds. And the teaching that the Buddha nature lives in all men is one of the clearest statements of the truth of the indwelling Adjusters ever made by a Urantian religion. The Buddhist mind moved through three stages toward the Absolute.
94.b47.t: Stage of the concept of the Absolute
The historic Siddhartha was gradually turned into a myth
Anyone might aspire to become a Buddha
All Buddhas are manifestations of one absolute source
94.b48.p: Such ideas were good for philosophy, but the book says that even an anthropomorphic Yahweh has greater religious value than a remote Absolute. For the masses, who were waiting for a promise that faith assures favor and survival, it was cold comfort.
94.b50.p: Buddhist cosmology had two weaknesses — it was contaminated by superstition, and it made Gautama a god — yet it kept evolving for twenty-five hundred years. Within the Mahayana there grew up a concept of Deity distinct from the Absolute, which finally bore fruit in Japan, in the teachings of Ryonin, Honen Shonin, and Shinran, as faith in Amida Buddha. Believers hold that whoever calls on the name of Amida with true faith and a pure heart will reach the happiness of the western Paradise.
94.b51.p: The great strength of Buddhism is that its followers are free to choose truth from any religion, and in the twentieth century Buddhism is experiencing a new renaissance. The book says that all Urantia is waiting for the message of Michael, unburdened by the doctrines piled up over nineteen centuries.
94.b53.p: Paper 94 follows the fate of the simple Salem gospel among the great religions and philosophies of the East. In India the priests rejected favor without sacrifices, and God became an impersonal Absolute. In China, Lao-tse and Confucius stood on Salem’s roots, but they were overshadowed by ancestor worship and superstition. Gautama preached a salvation freely given, but he too was exalted as a god. Yet within all these streams the seed of Salem survived, and it sprouted again in bright insights: the divinity within, the relativity of truth, and the mercy of Amida. What is needed now is not doctrines about Jesus but the gospel of Jesus itself, carried to the peoples of every faith.
94.b54.t: Section
Key message
1. The Salem Teachings in Vedic India
The Brahman priests rejected salvation by faith
2. Brahmanism
Priestly pride and the doctrine of reincarnation took away India’s hope
3. Brahmanic Philosophy
A noble philosophy that missed the personal God and the survival of the soul
4. The Hindu Religion
The most adaptable religion needs the living gospel of Jesus
5. The Struggle for Truth in China
The Salem teachings became the roots of early Taoism and Shinto
6. Lao-Tse and Confucius
In the sixth century B.C. the Salem gospel was revived
7. Gautama Siddhartha
A true prophet who preached a salvation freely given
8. The Buddhist Faith
The four truths and the eightfold path — but a salvation without God
9. The Spread of Buddhism
Spreading across Asia, it came more and more to resemble older religions
10. Religion in Tibet
Elements of every religion, but not the simple gospel of Jesus
11. Buddhist Philosophy
Bright insights: the divinity within and the relativity of truth
12. The God Concept of Buddhism
It bore fruit in faith in the mercy of Amida
94.b56.box: The Salem seed — that favor is received by faith — lives on, scattered through all the religions of the East, and the time has come to bring them the gospel of Jesus itself.
95.title: The Melchizedek Teachings in the Levant
95.b0.ask: “In the Levant, the cradle of Western faith, where did the Salem gospel fail, and through whom was it kept from going out?”
95.b2.p: In Paper 94 we saw what became of the Salem gospel in India, China, and East Asia. Paper 95 now turns westward to look at the Levant, the birthplace of the Western faiths.
95.b3.p: Just as India was the cradle of the religions and philosophies of East Asia, the Levant was the cradle of the faiths of the Western world. The Salem missionaries spread through Palestine, Mesopotamia, Egypt, Iran, and Arabia. In some places they bore rich fruit; in others their results were uneven. Sometimes they failed for lack of wisdom, sometimes because of circumstances beyond their control.
95.b4.p: Where, then, did the missionaries go wrong? And how did men like Amenemope, Ikhnaton, and Zoroaster pass the spark on to the ages that followed?
95.b5.q: ⟦Q 95:5.11⟧Never did the concept of monotheism die out of the hearts of men in Egypt and in the world.⟦/Q⟧
95.b8.p: By about 2000 B.C. the religion of Mesopotamia had all but lost the teachings of the Sethites. The Adamite custom of the seventh day survived, but it had become an unlucky day of taboos, and the Jews later carried those taboos into Palestine. The Salem teachers held the upper hand for more than a hundred and fifty years. They reduced the many gods to seven, and then to the triad of Bel, Ea, and Anu.
95.b9.p: But things went wrong when Nabodad, leader of the school at Kish, launched an all-out attack on the practice of temple prostitution. When the social reform failed, the spiritual teaching fell with it, and the worship of Ishtar and astrology flourished again. The missionaries had left their real task — preaching the gospel — and become entangled in reforming the mores.
95.b10.q: ⟦Q 95:1.8⟧But it has often been the error of the teachers of new truth to attempt too much, to attempt to supplant slow evolution by sudden revolution.⟦/Q⟧
95.b11.p: Even so, small scattered groups kept their belief in one Creator. The psalms they carved on stone were later found by Hebrew priests during the captivity and placed in the book of Psalms, and the Book of Job reflects well the teachings of the Salem school.
95.b13.p: The teachings of Melchizedek took deepest root in Egypt, and from there they spread to Europe. The Jews received their idea of creation from Babylonia and their idea of divine providence from Egypt. Egypt was more receptive for political rather than religious reasons. Every tribal leader who seized the throne proclaimed his own god the creator of all the others, and so the people gradually grew used to the idea of a supergod.
95.b14.p: The Egyptians believed that preserving the body helped the passage to the next world, so they developed embalming and burial statues, and they gathered magic formulas into the Book of the Dead. But early on they linked magic with conscience and character, and gradually they looked for salvation in ethical ideals rather than in tombs. They believed that a soul found innocent before the judgment hall of Osiris — free of murder, robbery, lying, adultery, theft, and selfishness — would enter the realms of bliss. For its time this was an advanced idea. The concept of judgment after death passed from Egypt into Hebrew theology.
95.b16.p: The book says that moral evolution does not depend wholly on revelation. Because a divine spirit dwells in man, he can also grow in spiritual values through his own experience. Egypt is the great example: thousands of years before the Salem gospel arrived, its moral leaders taught justice, fairness, and the avoidance of greed.
95.b17.t: The man whose standard is righteousness stands firm
Do right and deal justly with all
Life to the peaceful, death to the guilty
First proclaimed conscience as the voice of God
95.b18.p: The book judges that of all the purely human religions, none ever surpassed the social ideals and moral grandeur of this humanism of the Nile valley. Yet Egypt was intellectual and moral but not overly spiritual. Of the four great prophets who arose in six thousand years, Amenemope was followed for a season, Okhban was murdered, Ikhnaton was accepted halfheartedly, and Moses was rejected.
95.b20.p: Amenemope, also called the son of man, raised conscience to the highest standard of right and wrong. He believed that one should live every moment aware of God’s presence, and he taught his son honesty in public office. His great prayer was for freedom from fear, and he taught that man proposes, but God disposes.
95.b21.t: Chapters 15, 17, 20, and 22:17 to 24:22 are taken almost word for word
The first Psalm is Amenemope’s work
Translated into Greek, it influenced Hellenic religious philosophy
He owned a copy of the Book of Wisdom
95.b22.p: He was not the greatest teacher of his age, but he was the most influential, for he colored the thought of the two vital links of Western civilization: the Hebrews and the Greeks.
95.b24.p: A woman of the royal family, who had accepted the Melchizedek teachings through the influence of a Salemite physician, persuaded her son, the Pharaoh Ikhnaton. No one since Melchizedek had understood the Salem religion as clearly as he did. He kept open the channel of monotheism for the bestowal of Michael, and partly in recognition of this, the infant Jesus was taken to Egypt.
95.b25.p: Under the outward form of Aton, the sun-god, Ikhnaton led the people to worship the one God, the creator of Aton. He wrote the Book of the One God and one hundred and thirty-seven hymns, twelve of which survive in the Psalms. The most important word in his religion was righteousness.
95.b26.t: He built too fast, more than could survive after he was gone
He neglected the material security and prosperity of his people
They kept their cults in secret and revived them when he died
The idea of a Creator of all the world did not raise army morale
Only the educated understood; the peasants went back to Osiris
95.b27.p: After his death his son-in-law Tutankhamen returned to the old gods, but the wave of monotheism never died out completely. The democracy of salvation and resurrection for all men also won out in the end. Egypt passed on to the West both the evolutionary culture of the Nile and the revealed religion of the Euphrates, and the Hebrews carried many of Ikhnaton’s doctrines into their own religion.
95.b29.p: In Iran the Salem teachers made progress for more than five hundred years, but persecution under a change of rulers practically ended their work. Then, in the sixth century before Christ, Zoroaster appeared and rekindled the dying embers. At Ur he heard the story of the Seven Master Spirits and set up seven supreme gods with Ahura-Mazda at their head. His religion was a militant philosophy that centered on action more than on prayer or ritual.
95.b30.p: Zoroaster did not teach fire worship; he used fire as a symbol of the pure and wise Spirit. Original Zoroastrianism was not pure dualism, for in the eternal perspective evil was submerged in good. The Hebrew teachings about heaven, hell, and devils came mainly from Zoroastrianism during the period of Persian rule, and his teachings went on to influence Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.
95.b32.p: Even in Arabia, so close to Salem, the teachings of Melchizedek failed more completely than in China or Rome. Each tribe served its own fetish, and Ishtar, Yahweh, Ahura, and the Father of Jesus competed for a long time. The book says that the Christian missionaries of the desert were too strict. Had they preached more graciously, and been less stringent in the social demands they added, Arabia too would gladly have received the simple gospel of the carpenter’s son.
95.b33.p: Almost every tribe shared a common reverence for the black stone in the Kaaba at Mecca, and this later became the basis of Islam. The book explains that the strength of Islam has been its clear presentation of Allah as the one and only Deity, and its weakness the use of military force to spread it, together with the degradation of woman. Even so, Islam has steadfastly held to the concept of one universal God, merciful and compassionate.
95.b34.q: “⟦Q 95:7.6⟧For whenever as many as three speak together, God is present as a fourth,⟦/Q⟧”
95.b36.p: Paper 95 shows the road the Salem gospel traveled across the Levant. In Mesopotamia the missionaries hurried social reform and lost the gospel itself. In Egypt, on soil long prepared by moral teaching, Amenemope and Ikhnaton kept alive the spark of the one God. In Iran Zoroaster rekindled that light, and in Arabia, after long failure, faith in the one Allah grew up. Failure and success were mingled, yet these sparks flowed on through the Hebrews and the Greeks into the whole Western world, and at last prepared a place for the coming of Michael.
95.b37.t: By hurrying social reform, they lost the spiritual gospel too
From tombs and magic to an ethical judgment after death
Even without revelation, Egypt reached a high morality
His wisdom flowed into Proverbs, the Psalms, and Greek philosophy
He moved too fast, but he kept the flame of the one God alive
Zoroaster rekindled the fading light of Salem
After long failure, Islam was born, with its faith in one God
95.b39.box: Truth collapses when it is forced in haste, yet the spark of faith in one God is never put out; through a few men and women it is handed on to the next age.
96.title: Yahweh—God of the Hebrews
96.b0.ask: “How did the fearsome tribal god of the Sinai volcano grow into the concept of a loving and merciful Creator Father?”
96.b2.p: In Paper 95 we saw how the spark of Salem was carried, barely alive, across the Levant. Paper 96 now focuses on the people who held that spark most stubbornly: the Hebrews and their God, Yahweh.
96.b3.p: Men first accept all gods, then place the other gods under their own tribal god, and finally keep only the supreme One and let the rest go. But Melchizedek’s concept of God, unlike this evolutionary philosophy, was based on creative power alone. One purpose of Melchizedek’s incarnation was to foster a religion of one God and so prepare the way for the coming of a Son. Michael could come only if there were a people who believed in the Universal Father.
96.b4.p: The Hebrew religion was rooted in the covenant between Abraham and Melchizedek, and it took in the morality of Egypt, the theology of Babylon, and the Iranian ideas of good and evil. Through what twists and turns, then, did this people’s concept of God reach maturity?
96.b5.q: ⟦Q 96:4.9⟧The most unique and amazing feature of the religious history of the Hebrews concerns this continuous evolution of the concept of Deity⟦/Q⟧
96.b8.p: The early Semites believed that spirits dwelt in everything, and even the teachings of Melchizedek did not wholly do away with their belief in these nature gods. The Hebrews’ road from polytheism through henotheism to monotheism was not a straight line; there were many setbacks. So it helps first to sort out the various names for Deity.
96.b9.t: The nature god of the southern tribes, linked with Mount Horeb, the Sinai volcano
The Most High God of heaven taught by Melchizedek
A blend of the ideas of Amenemope, Ikhnaton, and Melchizedek
A name used for the various evolving ideas of Deity together
God as three in one — the concept of the Trinity
The Lord, the Almighty, the Most High, the Lord of hosts, the Father in heaven, and others
96.b10.p: The name Jehovah came into use much later, to stand for the completed concept of Yahweh. Mount Sinai was an intermittently active volcano, and its fire, smoke, and thunder filled the Bedouins with a great fear of Yahweh. The book says that the idea of Yahweh has undergone the most extensive development of all the mortal theories of God. The Jews changed their view of him from a tribal god to a merciful Creator Father, but they never changed his name.
96.b12.p: The Semites included the eastern Semites, allied with Babylonia; the Phoenicians along the Mediterranean coast; and the Arabian Semites, who kept pressing in from the north. The book explains that the Semites were among the most blended of peoples, carrying elements of nearly all nine races. Bedouins who entered Egypt in a time of famine went through the bitter experience of slavery there.
96.b13.p: Abraham was not the ancestor of all the Hebrews. Most of the clans of Israel had never been in Egypt; they were fellow nomads who chose to follow Moses. During the years of bondage the covenant of Melchizedek was largely forgotten, and the religion of the masses was the old Yahweh cult of magic and sacrifice.
96.b15.p: The real growth of the Hebrew concept of God began with the exodus led by Moses. His mother was of the Egyptian royal family, and his father was a Semitic liaison officer. The book explains that his very mixed ancestry gave him an unusual adaptability for leading a varied multitude. He turned away from the lure of the culture of the Nile and cast his lot with his father’s people.
96.b16.p: No leader ever tried to lift up a more forsaken and dispirited band than did Moses. He first won, through diplomacy, the promise of a peaceful departure, but when the king broke the treaty, Moses seized the moment when the Egyptian army was busy fighting off Libyan and Greek attacks and led his people out in a carefully planned escape by night.
96.b18.p: Moses learned of El Shaddai from his parents and of El Elyon from his Kenite father-in-law, and he decided to proclaim a new and larger concept of God that combined the two, presenting it as an enlarged idea of Yahweh, the old tribal god. He judged that the slaves would never understand El Elyon, so he chose a compromise: to make the desert tribal god the only God.
96.b19.p: In the third week of their stay at Sinai, Mount Horeb erupted violently, and Moses could easily impress on the people that God was a mighty and terrible consuming fire. He nationalized Yahweh as the jealous God of a chosen people, yet he also worked to broaden their concept, teaching that Yahweh was the God of the spirits of all flesh and a covenant-keeping God.
96.b20.q: “⟦Q 96:4.6⟧The eternal God is your refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms.⟦/Q⟧”
96.b21.p: In this way Yahweh, a tribal god, became the God of Israel, who followed his people into the wilderness and even into exile, and through the Babylonian captivity he finally became the God of all nations.
96.b23.p: Moses was military leader, social organizer, and religious teacher all in one, and he was the most important world teacher between the times of Machiventa and Jesus. Many of his advances were due to the Kenite traditions surviving from the days of Melchizedek. With his father-in-law Jethro he gathered those traditions and, choosing the best of Egypt and Palestine, organized the Hebrew system of worship.
96.b24.t: To whom, and of what kind
To the leaders — there is none beside him
To the multitude — who is like your God among all the gods?
One who prospers those who obey
Awe of justice was stressed more than mercy
No images of any sort were to be made
96.b25.p: The book says it was truly pitiful to watch Moses trying to adapt his sublime concept to the level of an ignorant people. The Hebrews of this age learned little of God’s mercy, and when Moses died most of them went back to worshiping the golden calf. Even so, he gathered many tribes together and laid the foundation of a self-sustaining nation.
96.b26.h: 6. The God Concept after Moses’ Death
96.b27.p: After Moses died, his lofty concepts declined quickly. The leaders kept his traditions, but the common people returned to the old desert Yahweh, and the decline went on through the times of the judges. Settled in Palestine as farmers, they almost lost the chance to keep monotheism and the teachings of Melchizedek alive while the thundering desert god was slowly changing into a God of love and mercy.
96.b28.p: Joshua preached Yahweh sternly, as a holy and jealous God. Yet even in that dark age a solitary teacher would arise now and then to proclaim the concept of Moses: that God is great, and we cannot fully know him.
96.b29.h: 7. Psalms and the Book of Job
96.b30.p: Once settled in Palestine, the Hebrews fell into idolatry and license, and their concept of God sank far below the Egyptian and Mesopotamian concepts kept by the Salem groups. Those higher concepts are preserved in the Psalms and the Book of Job.
96.b31.t: Written by more than twenty authors, a record from Amenemope to Isaiah
A spirit of worship that surpasses all the other sacred books of the world
The work of Mesopotamian teachers over about three hundred years
In a dark age, the idea of the true God was kept alive near Ur
96.b32.p: In Palestine the wisdom and omnipresence of God were known, but his love and mercy were hardly known at all. Only at Ur did Elihu, priest of the Salem believers, cry out salvation by faith: that God is gracious to the repentant. In this way the descendants of the Salem missionaries kept the light of truth alive until the long line of Israel’s teachers arose to complete the concept of a universal Creator Father.
96.b33.q: “⟦Q 96:7.7⟧He shall pray to God and shall find favor with him and shall see his face with joy, for God will give to man divine righteousness.⟦/Q⟧”
96.b35.p: Paper 96 shows how slow and winding the road was by which one people’s concept of God matured. Yahweh, the fearsome tribal god of the Sinai volcano, was clothed by Moses in the garments of the one God, but the people could not bear it and slipped back again and again. Yet the scattered descendants of Salem, solitary teachers, and the authors of the Psalms and Job kept the light burning. To the end the name remained Yahweh, but the One to whom that name pointed was little by little growing into the God of all nations, the loving and merciful Creator Father.
96.b36.t: Many names and ideas of Deity blended and gathered under Yahweh
During the Egyptian bondage, Melchizedek’s covenant was largely forgotten
He led a forsaken band of slaves out to freedom
Moses presented a higher God under the name of the old tribal god
He struggled to fit a sublime concept to an ignorant people
6. The God Concept after Moses’ Death
The people slipped back, but solitary teachers kept the light
7. Psalms and the Book of Job

96.b38.box: To the end the name was Yahweh, but the God it pointed to grew from a fearsome tribal god into the merciful Father of all nations.
97.title: Evolution of the God Concept among the Hebrews
97.b0.ask: “From Samuel to the second Isaiah, how did the prophets of Israel, step by step, reveal God as the loving Father of all peoples?”
97.b2.p: In Paper 96 we saw how Yahweh, the tribal god of Sinai, was clothed by Moses in the garments of the one God — and how the people slipped back once Moses was gone. Paper 97 now follows the prophets who came after him, and shows how they raised this idea up again and kept widening it.
97.b3.p: The paper says that the spiritual leaders of the Hebrews did something no one before them had managed. They took the human features out of their idea of God, yet they did not turn him into an abstraction that only philosophers could grasp. Even common people could think of Yahweh as a Father — if not of each person, at least of the race. Above all, the sense of God as a person grew almost without a break from Moses to Malachi, and at last it was heightened and glorified by the teachings of Jesus.
97.b4.p: So whose courage made this growth possible? And what was the real history that unfolded alongside it?
97.b5.q: ⟦Q 97:7.9⟧God would not forget, would not forsake.⟦/Q⟧
97.b8.p: When pressure from hostile neighbors pushed the tribes to unite under a central government, Samuel had his opportunity. He came from a long line of the Salem teachers. He was a rough-and-ready reformer who acted more than he preached — a man who could go out in a single day and overthrow a score of Baal sites. Even so, he won back to the higher idea of Yahweh only the more intelligent half of the Hebrews.
97.b9.p: Samuel’s great contribution was his ringing announcement that Yahweh does not change. Until then Yahweh had been pictured as a fitful God, always regretting what he had done. Samuel also gave hope to the lowly by proclaiming that God raises the poor out of the dust, and in his later years he even declared that God’s mercies are great. Yet his God was still chiefly concerned with the Hebrews, his chosen people.
97.b10.q: “⟦Q 97:1.4⟧The Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent, for he is not a man, that he should repent.⟦/Q⟧”
97.b12.p: In the tenth century before Christ the Hebrew nation split into two kingdoms, and spiritual decline set in. Elijah, a fearless warrior for righteousness, restored to the northern kingdom an idea of God like the one held in Samuel’s day. But he was so busy tearing down the altars of Baal in the face of an idolatrous king that he had little chance to teach anything higher. Elisha, his faithful associate, took up the work and, with the help of the little-known Micaiah, kept the light of truth alive. The paper says this was not a time of progress. It was a time of recovery, when the idea of the Universal Creator was brought back to about where Samuel had left it.
97.b14.p: The paper explains that the long struggle between Yahweh and Baal was less a difference in religious belief than a socioeconomic clash over land.
97.b15.t: A gift of Deity to the clan; it could not be sold
Yahweh, to whom the land belonged
Baal, “owner,” the god of rain and fertile soil
97.b16.p: It was Elijah who turned this quarrel into a religious issue. When Ahab murdered the Naboths to get their land, Elijah made a moral issue out of the old land customs and launched his campaign against the Baalites. It was also a fight of country people against the rule of the cities. The Baals were many, but Yahweh was one — and monotheism won over polytheism.
97.b18.p: Amos was not just a restorer; he discovered new truths about God. For the first time since Melchizedek, people heard the double standard of national justice condemned: Yahweh would no more tolerate sin among his own people than among any other nation. Amos proclaimed Yahweh the “⟦Q 97:4.4|97:6.2|97:7.1⟧God of all nations⟦/Q⟧” and warned that ritual must not take the place of righteousness. For this he was stoned to death.
97.b19.p: Hosea followed Amos’s God of justice and brought back the Mosaic idea of a God of love. He preached forgiveness through repentance, not by sacrifice.
97.b20.t: What he added to the idea of God
A God of universal justice who punishes sin even among the chosen people
A God of love and mercy who forgives those who repent
97.b21.p: Amos woke the conscience of the nation; Hosea struck the opening notes of the divine compassion and loving-kindness that Isaiah would later sing so beautifully.
97.b23.p: In this time of awakened conscience the first Isaiah appeared. He preached the eternal nature of God, his infinite wisdom, and his unchanging reliability. He declared that sins as red as scarlet shall be as white as snow, and he sang of good tidings — of binding up the brokenhearted and proclaiming liberty to the captives.
97.b24.p: After him came Micah and Obadiah, who boldly attacked the priest-ridden ritual and the whole system of sacrifice. Micah rebuked the priests who taught for hire, and he pictured a day when every man would sit under his own vine with no one to make him afraid. The paper says that, but for the stubborn resistance of the priests, these teachers would have overthrown the whole bloody ceremonial of Hebrew worship.
97.b25.q: “⟦Q 97:5.6⟧He has shown me, O man, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justly and to love mercy and to walk humbly with your God?⟦/Q⟧”
97.b27.p: Jeremiah took the next bold step in making Yahweh the God of all peoples. He declared that Yahweh was not on the side of the Hebrews in their wars, but was God of all the earth, of all nations and all peoples. There was no Osiris for the Egyptians, no Bel for the Babylonians, no Ashur for the Assyrians. With this the idea of Yahweh rose to a level of planetary and even cosmic dignity.
97.b28.p: He also preached that God loves us with an everlasting love. But when he counseled surrender during the siege of Jerusalem, the priests and rulers cast him into a miry pit.
97.b30.p: When the nation fell and its people were carried off to Babylon, the priests, resenting the loss of their national god, inflated their history and multiplied miracles to restore the Jews as the chosen people. The paper adds that they did not claim to write by inspiration or to produce a sacred book; they were simply preparing a textbook to bolster the courage of their fellow captives.
97.b31.p: Then a young prophet appeared: the second Isaiah. He embraced the first Isaiah’s God of love and mercy and Jeremiah’s God of all nations, and he won converts among both the Jews and their Babylonian captors. His writings survive in chapters forty to fifty-five of the book of Isaiah. The paper says that no teacher from Machiventa to Jesus reached a concept of God as high as his.
97.b32.t: The God of the second Isaiah
“⟦Q 97:7.6⟧I am the first and the last; there is no God beside me.⟦/Q⟧”
“⟦Q 97:7.6⟧Fear you not, for I am with you.⟦/Q⟧”
A Father who does not forget
“⟦Q 97:7.7⟧I have graven them upon the palms of my hands.⟦/Q⟧”
“⟦Q 97:7.8⟧He shall gather the lambs in his arms and carry them in his bosom.⟦/Q⟧”
“⟦Q 97:7.12⟧I dwell in the high and holy place, also with him who is of a contrite and humble spirit.⟦/Q⟧”
97.b33.p: Isaiah eclipsed the jealous Yahweh of the desert with his picture of the ruler of the universe and affectionate Father of all mankind. Ever since, the highest idea of God in the West has embraced universal justice, divine mercy, and eternal righteousness. Yet because the priests clung to a narrow nationalism, the teaching of the two Isaiahs did not fully prepare the way to receive the Messiah.
97.b35.p: The paper says that the habit of treating the Hebrew record as sacred history, and the affairs of the rest of the world as profane history, has caused much confusion. After the Babylonian priests prepared their new record, they destroyed the older ones, such as “⟦Q 97:8.1⟧The Doings of the Kings of Israel.⟦/Q⟧” The Jews wrestled with the belief that the righteous are rewarded and sinners punished; the drama of Job was a protest against it, and Ecclesiastes a worldly wise reaction to it.
97.b36.p: Under five hundred years of foreign rule, the promises of the prophets seemed to point in different directions, and repeated false hopes led to deep frustration. As a result, the Jewish leaders failed to recognize a Son of Paradise when he came as the Son of Man. The paper grants that God has many times thrust a Father’s hand into human affairs — but that does not turn secular history into sacred history.
97.b38.p: The paper briefly shows how key parts of Hebrew history were reshaped in Babylon. There were never twelve tribes; only three or four settled in Palestine, and the Hebrew nation arose from a union of the Israelites and the Canaanites. Saul was made king by his troops, not by a priest, and the greatest distortions of all had to do with David.
97.b39.t: Only three or four tribes settled in Palestine
They were never driven out; the peoples intermarried
An army of a little more than three thousand
Their own troops and followers made them king
A kingdom built from a motley following and political marriages
97.b40.p: Then came the tyranny and luxury of David and Solomon, the split into two kingdoms and their wars, and the gathering of land into the hands of city nobles. When free speech was suppressed, Elijah, Amos, and Hosea began their secret writing — the real beginning of the Bible. The northern kingdom fell to Assyria and Judah to Babylon, and the shock of captivity drove the remnant into monotheism.
97.b41.p: The Jewish religion of the Old Testament really took shape in Babylon during the captivity. So did the sense of mission as Yahweh’s chosen servants, and the doctrine of immortality. The paper sums it up: Judaism was the soil out of which Christianity grew, but the Jews were not a miraculous people.
97.b43.p: Their leaders taught that Israel was chosen not for a monopoly of divine favor, but for the service of carrying the truth of the one God to every nation. Yet those who returned from exile bound themselves to the priests’ laws and rituals and set aside the magnificent concept of the second Isaiah. From then until John the Baptist, Israel slid backward spiritually. Even so, the Jews never lost the concept of the Universal Father.
97.b44.p: From Moses to John the Baptist an unbroken line of faithful teachers passed the monotheistic torch from one generation to the next. The Jewish religion was weak in philosophy and in beauty, but it conserved moral values, and so it endured; its institutions helped it last as well. The paper says it is better to reform ritual than to destroy it all, and it praises Ezekiel for his wisdom in this.
97.b45.p: In this way the teachers of Israel achieved the greatest feat in the evolution of religion: they moved from the jealous spirit god of the Sinai volcano to the creator of all things and the loving and merciful Father of all mankind. This was humanity’s highest picture of the Universal Father until it was enlarged by the teachings and life of Michael.
97.b47.p: Paper 97 shows how one people’s idea of God grew in the hands of its prophets. Samuel said that God does not change; Elijah set up the one God in place of Baal. Amos added justice and Hosea forgiveness; Jeremiah raised Yahweh to the God of all nations; and the second Isaiah sang of him as a shepherd who carries his lambs and as the Father of all mankind. The real history around them was ordinary and troubled, quite unlike the sacred history the priests composed. Yet within that very history, faithful teachers handed on the torch without a break — and in Jesus that torch finally burned brightest.
97.b48.t: God does not change, and he raises the poor

A struggle over land ended in the triumph of monotheism
To the God of justice was added the God of forgiveness and mercy
Do justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God
Yahweh is God of all nations and all the earth
The highest idea of God before Jesus: the Father of all mankind
The priests’ sacred history hid the real history

From the spirit god of Sinai to the merciful Father of mankind
97.b50.box: Passing the torch from generation to generation, the prophets of Israel revealed the fearsome tribal god of Sinai as the loving and merciful Father of all mankind.
98.title: The Melchizedek Teachings in the Occident
98.b0.ask: “How did Salem’s teaching of the one God make its way through the philosophies and mystery cults of the West until it reached Christianity?”
98.b2.p: In the earlier papers we followed Machiventa Melchizedek’s Salem teachings as they spread through the Levant and the East. Paper 98 now traces how those teachings flowed westward into Europe. They came chiefly by way of Egypt, and they were taken into Western philosophy after being thoroughly Hellenized and later Christianized.
98.b3.p: For a long time the Salem missionaries worked in Europe, but little by little they were absorbed into the many cults and ritual groups that rose and fell. The Cynics kept the Salem teachings in their purest form, and Jewish mercenary soldiers also spread the Salem doctrine across the West. So the basic doctrines of Greek philosophy, Jewish theology, and Christian ethics were at bottom echoes of the earlier Melchizedek teachings.
98.b4.p: What, then, did this teaching of the one God lose, and what did it keep, as it passed in turn through Greek philosophy, the Roman state religion, and the mystery cults of the East?
98.b5.q: ⟦Q 98:2.8⟧In Greece, believing was subordinated to thinking; in Palestine, thinking was held subject to believing.⟦/Q⟧
98.b7.h: 1. The Salem Religion among the Greeks
98.b8.p: The Salem missionaries kept strictly to the oath of ordination that Machiventa had imposed on them. They were not to organize exclusive congregations, never to function as priests, and never to take fees — only food, clothing, and shelter. Because they held so strictly to this pledge, they built no great religious structure in Greece. Meanwhile their teaching became mixed with the beliefs of later arrivals and slid back into a crude animism with bloody rites.
98.b9.p: Then the Hellenic invaders of the Aryan line brought in their manlike ideas of God, and the Greek family of gods and goddesses began to take shape. They set Dyaus-Zeus at the head of the pantheon. The Greeks might have reached a true monotheism in Zeus, had they not kept the overcontrol of Fate. But the gods of Olympus were more human than divine, and the intelligent Greeks never took them very seriously. Thanks to the antipriestcraft doctrines of the Salem teachers, no priesthood of any importance ever arose in Greece.
98.b10.t: The oath of the Salem teachers
No priesthood arose, and no organized religious structure
The god ideas of the Hellenic invaders
A family of gods formed, with Zeus at its head
Belief in the overcontrol of Fate
The concept of Zeus fell short of a true monotheism
A mythology more aesthetic than ethic
Morals and philosophy advanced far beyond the god concept, creating an imbalance
98.b12.p: The Olympian religion promised no salvation, and within a thousand years it had nearly vanished. When the East experienced a monotheistic awakening in the sixth century before Christ, the West did not take part. Instead the Greeks made a magnificent intellectual advance and sought comfort for the soul in philosophy and metaphysics. But they did not see that true religion is the cure for soul hunger and moral despair.
98.b13.p: The philosophers scorned worship, yet nearly all of them held loosely to the Salem doctrine of “⟦Q 98:2.4⟧the Intelligence of the universe⟦/Q⟧” and “⟦Q 98:2.4|15:1.6|27:1.5⟧the Great Source.⟦/Q⟧” Xenophanes taught one God, but his idea was too pantheistic. Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle taught that virtue is knowledge and that it is wrong to return evil for evil. The paper draws a sharp contrast between Greece and Palestine.
98.b14.t: Almost no priests or sacred scriptures; the mind was free
Thought was wholly priest-controlled and scripture-directed
Thinking was held subject to believing
The idea of God dissolved into a mist of pantheism
Dogma hardened until further growth was in danger
98.b15.p: Ordinary people did not want abstract philosophy; they wanted promises of salvation and a personal God who could hear their prayers. So Greece plunged quickly into the mystery cults — the Eleusinian mysteries, the worship of Dionysus, the Orphic brotherhood. The paper says the ideal is for philosophy, religion, and science to be welded into one through wisdom, faith, and experience.
98.b16.q: ⟦Q 98:2.12⟧Philosophy is to religion as conception is to action.⟦/Q⟧
98.b18.p: Latin religion grew from the worship of family gods into the tribal reverence for Mars, the god of war, and it remained largely a political observance. Too few Salem missionaries reached Italy, and those who did could not overcome the Etruscan priesthood. Roman religion consisted mostly of mere forms, vows, and taboos. Most of the Greek gods were carried over as well, with new names.
98.b19.t: Hestia, virgin goddess of the hearth
98.b20.p: Rome conquered politically, but it was in turn conquered by the cults of Egypt, Greece, and the Levant. When Augustus heard how the Salem teachers had tried to spread the doctrine of one God, he re-established the state religion — and then proclaimed himself the supreme god. In time the official cult listed more than two-score self-elevated human deities. The last stand of the Salem believers was made by the Cynics, but most people preferred the mysteries, which also satisfied their craving for excitement and entertainment.
98.b22.p: Having lost their family and state religions, and unable to grasp Greek philosophy, most people of the Greco-Roman world turned to the mystery cults of Egypt and the Levant. These promised comfort for today and hope of immortality after death. Three became the most popular.
98.b23.t: Cybele and her son Attis — imposing but degrading, with bloody festivals
Osiris and his mother Isis — more refined and impressive
Mithras, savior and redeemer of sinful mankind
98.b24.p: The Phrygian and Egyptian mysteries taught that the divine son had died and been raised again, and that those properly initiated, who kept the anniversary of his death and resurrection, would share in his divine nature and immortality. The Osiris legend grew from watching the plants die back each year and come to life again in spring. Yet the frenzy and orgies of these cults were sometimes most revolting.
98.b26.p: The worship of Mithras was the greatest of all the mystery cults, and it displaced the other two. Roman legions recruited in the Levant carried it everywhere they went. The cult arose in Iran, and by the time it reached Rome it had absorbed many of Zoroaster’s teachings. It was chiefly through Mithraism that Zoroaster’s religion influenced Christianity.
98.b27.t: A warrior god born from a great rock; a last supper with the sun-god before he ascended into the heavens
In caves, three times a day, with weekly ceremonies on the day of the sun-god
The annual festival of Mithras on December twenty-fifth
The sacrament was believed to ensure eternal life; there would be a last judgment
At first for men only, with seven orders entered one after another
98.b28.p: Later the wives and daughters of believers were admitted to the temples of the Great Mother, which stood next to the Mithraic temples. The women’s cult mixed Mithraic ritual with the ceremonies of Cybele.
98.b30.p: Before the mystery cults and Christianity, religion in the West was mainly a matter of family, city-state, and empire; personal religion hardly grew into an institution of its own. The paper notes that institutions often weaken the spiritual quality of religion — yet no religion has survived without some degree of institutional organization. In the third century after Christ, Mithraic and Christian churches looked very much alike, both in appearance and in ritual.
98.b31.t: Underground worship, holy water, baptism, bread and wine
Underground worship, holy water, baptism, bread and wine
Admitted women into the full fellowship of the faith
98.b32.p: The deciding factor in the contest between the two was that Christianity admitted women. In the end, in the West, Greek philosophy supplied the concepts of ethical value; Mithraism, the ritual of worship; and Christianity, the technique for conserving moral and social values.
98.b34.p: A Creator Son did not take on mortal flesh to reconcile an angry God, but to win all mankind to the recognition of the Father’s love and to the realization of their sonship with God. Christianity is built around the person of Jesus of Nazareth, the incarnate Michael Son of Nebadon. Yet as a system of belief, Christianity arose from the blending of many elements.
98.b35.t: A basic factor in all the religions of East and West for four thousand years
Morality, ethics, theology, and belief in Providence and the supreme Yahweh
The idea of a struggle between cosmic good and evil
Mithraism and the worship of the Great Mother
The human life of Joshua ben Joseph and the glorified Christ
Mithraism was the dominant religion of Tarsus in his youth
Joined with Paul’s theology, it still forms the basis of European ethics
98.b36.p: As the teachings of Jesus became Westernized, they began to lose their appeal to all races and kinds of men. Christianity glorified Jesus as the Messiah, but it largely forgot the Master’s personal gospel: the Fatherhood of God and the universal brotherhood of all men. Even so, Machiventa achieved the purpose of his bestowal. When Michael came, the God concept was alive in human hearts — and it still flames anew in living spiritual experience today.
98.b37.q: ⟦Q 98:7.11⟧It has long since ceased to be the religion of Jesus, although it still valiantly portrays a beautiful religion about Jesus⟦/Q⟧
98.b39.p: Paper 98 shows the winding road Salem’s teaching of the one God traveled in the West. Greece thought freely without priests but placed faith beneath thought; Rome turned religion into a ritual of the state; and people hungry for salvation flocked to the mystery cults. Among these, Mithraism and Christianity contended, and Christianity, which welcomed women, won the West. Yet through all these twists and turns, the God concept Machiventa planted never went out. Though Christianity has forgotten much of Jesus’ personal gospel, the Fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man still burn anew in the experience of those who sincerely walk his way.
98.b40.t: 1. The Salem Religion among the Greeks
A teaching without priests lost ground to a family of gods
Greece put faith beneath thought; Palestine put thought beneath faith
Rome conquered by politics, but was conquered in turn by the Eastern cults

Christianity, which admitted women, won the contest
